newsitem.title: USA: Texas clears hurdle to offshore crude oil terminal.
newsitem.headline: Texas clears hurdle to offshore crude oil terminal.

text.p: Federal regulators have approved the Texas coastal management plan, clearing the way for state ports to seek permits to build offshore crude oil shipping terminals, regulators said on Wednesday.

Port authorities in Corpus Christi and refiners near Galveston have studied the feasibility of offshore ports, where tankers can offload crude oil that is transferred by pipeline to onshore refineries, officials said.
"We were very close to kicking ours off here," engineer Jim Shiner said of a $100 million plan to construct an offshore oil port off the coast of Corpus Christi.
The $100 million project would cost well less than $500 million needed to dredge a channel for deep-draft tankers, and would be safer than existing lightering operations, he said.

But the project was shelved when local refineries began taking more deliveries from Mexico and Venezuela shipped in smaller tankers. "The project isn't cancelled, it's just on the shelf," said Shiner, whose Shiner Moseley & Associates engineer firm drafted plans for the offshore port.

The Louisiana Offshore Oil Port, the nation's lone U.S. deepwater crude oil terminal, operates about 20 miles off the coast of Grand Isle, Louisiana. Reversing a five-year decline. The LOOP last year moved 820,000 barrels per day of crude oil.

Approval of the Texas coastal management plan is not expected to jump-start any offshore port proposals, but the state's new deepwater port status clears a major hurdle in the process of gaining federal approval for a proposed terminal.
Plans for offshore oil ports have been put on the shelf in Texas recently as more oil arrives in relatively smaller, short-haul tankers, officials said.
But the resumption of exports from Iraq and recent discoveries in Colombia could revive use of larger, deep-draft tankers and make the offshore oil ports economically viable, officials said.
